title: Macklemore vs. Robert Kraft
dek: Two nights at MetLife, one phone call from Robert Kraft, and the biggest tour on earth lost its opener. Then the opener booked his own. How a stadium veto turned a pop tour into a fight over Gaza, and why it isn't over.
body: The call came on a Monday. On September 7, according to Macklemore, Ed Sheeran told him privately that Robert Kraft had been on the phone. The New England Patriots owner would not let the Seattle rapper perform at Gillette Stadium, and other stadium owners felt the same way. Keep Macklemore, Sheeran was told, and the tour could lose the buildings.

A week later Macklemore was off the tour. Within a day, three other opening acts and the Irish band that played inside Sheeran's own set had quit. Two nights in New Jersey had become a national argument about Palestine, antisemitism, free expression, and who actually controls a stadium stage.
It still isn't over. Macklemore has booked his own benefit shows in Europe, Sheeran has rebuilt his lineup, and now even the charities on Macklemore's new tour are under fire.
## The song that came first

None of this should have surprised anyone. Ben Haggerty released "Hind's Hall" on May 6, 2024, named for the Columbia University building protesters renamed after Hind Rajab, a Palestinian child killed in Gaza. The track sampled Lebanese singer Fairuz and sent its streaming money to UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees.

Seattle saw the next chapter up close. At a Palestine benefit in Seward Park on September 21, 2024, he shouted "Fuck America" from the stage. The Kraken and Sounders criticized him, and a Las Vegas festival dropped him. He later said his anger had gotten ahead of his message. Anyone booking Macklemore in 2026 knew exactly where he stood.
## Two nights in New Jersey

Friday, September 4, MetLife Stadium. Before "Hind's Hall," Macklemore called for Palestinian freedom while the screens behind him showed footage from Gaza, the West Bank and protest marches. His speech ran wider than the headline: Lebanon, Cuba, Congo, Sudan, Iran, and a shot at Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Saturday, he came back and spoke to Jewish fans in the crowd directly. "Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you," he said, framing it as a matter of equal dignity. Critics heard hostility in the words and the imagery. Supporters heard a needed line drawn between Jewish people and Israel's government.

By Sunday, the Israeli-American Council was petitioning for his removal. The petition went after Sheeran, his management and the venues, asking whether the speech, the footage and the song had been approved in advance. It wasn't just about Macklemore anymore. It was about what anyone could say on that stage.

Pink weighed in next. She shared a StopAntisemitism post demanding apologies and refunds, then clarified on September 11. She pointed to Macklemore's 2014 costume, a fake nose and beard he had apologized for after it was called an antisemitic caricature, and described Jewish fans who felt afraid. But she was explicit: "I don't need anyone fired, and I don't need a refund." She also wrote that Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity.
## The owners' box

The Wall Street Journal later reported that Kraft's call to Sheeran lasted 40 minutes. The two are close; Sheeran sang at Kraft's 2022 wedding. The Journal also named three more NFL owners who opposed Macklemore's appearances: Carolina's David Tepper, Atlanta's Arthur Blank and Philadelphia's Jeffrey Lurie, describing calls between owners, with Lurie landing where Tepper and Blank already were.

On September 14, the promoter, Messina Touring Group, made it official. Venues had told it the shows couldn't go on with Macklemore on the bill, putting the rest of the tour at risk. He had been booked for eight of the ten remaining U.S. dates, starting September 19 in Philadelphia.

Macklemore's statement that day described painful conversations with a friend of 13 years and a basic disagreement about neutrality. He accused critics of using charges of antisemitism to shield Israeli policy, while saying antisemitism itself is real. And he refused the victim role. He, Sheeran and Pink would all go home safe to their families, he wrote; Palestinians were living the actual catastrophe.
"I didn't need 10 shows from Ed. I needed 2."

Kraft answered the same day. He cited the New Jersey shows and what he called a longer record of rhetoric and imagery offensive to Jews. He acknowledged Palestinian suffering, argued that Macklemore left out Hamas's responsibility, and offered to meet with him. His statement did not say whether he had organized the other owners. Kraft's stance has a long public track record: in 2019 he founded the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism with $20 million, now called the Blue Square Alliance Against Hate.
## "I am not complicit"

Sheeran spoke on September 15. Macklemore's contract was with the promoter, he said, and the promoter made the call. He said he had tried to mediate with the owners and owed it to ticket holders and his crew to keep the tour running. "I am not complicit," he wrote.

His lineup didn't buy it. The same day, Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham and Finneas pulled out, along with Beoga, the Irish band that played during Sheeran's own set. Finneas had been booked for the South American leg in November, not the U.S. dates. "Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," he wrote. Rowe pointed to Ireland's own history of famine and occupation. Beoga, co-founders of Irish Artists for Palestine, said they still counted Sheeran a friend. Every one of them was walking away from a stadium audience.
## The money

On September 16, Macklemore pledged all $1 million of his net tour earnings to six groups: Palestine Children's Relief Fund, HEAL Palestine, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, UNRWA USA and Anera. He dared Kraft to match it, and said writing a check is one of the cheapest ways to show solidarity.

Kraft came back with a bigger number. He said Sheeran had already asked him to commit $2 million to match Sheeran's own gift for humanitarian relief in the region. KIRO 7 pointed out that the wording described a request, not a promise, and named no recipients and no timeline.

The next day, Ms. Rachel, the children's star Rachel Accurso, said she would match Macklemore's million too, and named where it was going: Palestine Children's Relief Fund, where she is an ambassador.
## The show goes on

Sheeran played Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field on September 19 with no opener. Reading from prepared remarks, he apologized for mistakes, condemned the October 7 attacks, called Gaza "catastrophic and unjustifiable," and spoke against injustice in the West Bank and against venues approving performers and content in advance. He said the whole thing made him wonder if he wanted to keep doing this. Protesters stood outside. The man who wanted to stay out of politics was now making a political speech every night.
The Gillette shows that started it all never happened. A nor'easter canceled both nights on September 25. In early October, Zach Bryan played that same stadium in a "Free Palestine" shirt.

Sheeran rebuilt the bill. Isaac Slade, formerly of The Fray, opened in Atlanta on October 3 and is booked for more dates, including Charlotte on October 17, Arlington on October 24 and Tampa on November 7. American Idol's Brooks Rosser joined in Indianapolis on October 10. The tour survived. The fight follows every lineup announcement.
## The Free Palestine Tour

Macklemore's answer came September 24. The Free Palestine Tour: Dublin's 3Arena on October 26, Paris's Accor Arena on October 29, London's OVO Arena Wembley on October 30, billed as Macklemore and Friends, with all proceeds going to Palestinian causes and U.S. dates promised. On September 30 he said all three had sold out.

The beneficiary list grew to twelve. Beside the original six: Glia, Taawon, Middle East Children's Alliance, Jewish Voice for Peace, the Institute for Middle East Understanding and the Palestinian Youth Movement. Some of those are advocacy groups, not aid charities, which makes this a political fundraiser as much as a relief concert. His own site says the tour supports Palestinians and their movement.

That drew the newest fire. On October 16, The Jewish Chronicle reported that Britain's Jewish Leadership Council had challenged the Palestinian Youth Movement's inclusion, citing a British spokesperson's description of Hamas's October 7 hostage-taking as legitimate and effective, and asked Live Nation what vetting governs the money. Those are claims and questions, not findings that any concert money has funded violence. The Chronicle said it asked Macklemore and Live Nation for comment and reported no answer from either.
The real questions now are practical: how the proceeds get split, how much reaches each group, and when anyone will show the receipts. A sellout proves demand. It doesn't answer those.
## Back to Seattle

For Seattle it's tempting to make this simple: hometown hero versus billionaire. The record is more interesting. Stadium owners used a veto. A promoter enforced it. Fellow musicians walked. And the man they pushed off the stage found other rooms to fill.
Dublin is next. The microphone is his again, and so is everything that comes with it.
